posts.title: An Unc Responds
posts.description: The other day I checked Rootring and happened upon a fascinating post by a terrifyingly young Indonesian game designer named Roseline. Entitled “I’m a NewGen in a Hobby full of Uncs and That’s Okay” , the post is basically Roseline trying to orient herself in the broader TTRPG landscape and come to terms with the fact that while the hobby has attracted a load of younger players in recent years, it still appears rather old, white, and male when you look at the people hanging out on forums and going to conventions. As someone who quite often sits down to write about stuff in order to work out what I think, I recognise the exploratory nature of Roseline’s piece and I find it to be a wonderfully lucid, thoughtful, and generous account of what the hobby looks like when viewed from their perspective. posts.title: REVIEW: Strange Pictures (2025)
posts.description: Earlier this year I reviewed Strange Houses by the masked Japanese YouTuber, author, and song-writer Uketsu . While my experiences with the book were ultimately frustrating and unsatisfying, I must admit that the form of Strange Houses has remained with me and that this moved me to take another look at his work. First published in 2022, Strange Pictures is Uketsu’s second novel but was translated and released in English before Strange Houses . This was a bold (and I would argue wise) move as while the two novels are very similar, Strange Pictures is undoubtedly the more polished of the two. Taking its cues from Uketsu’s YouTube channel, the novel is positioned somewhere between mystery and horror; telling a story centred upon a series of images that only grow weirder and more interconnected the longer you look at them. posts.title: On “My Case for Retributive Action” by Thomas Ligotti
posts.description: Canon Fodder is an occasional series in which I write about classic works of horror fiction. This particular part of the series is devoted to the complete published works of Thomas Ligotti which I will slowly be working my way through. What if the horrors of corporate life were not something to which we might eventually acclimatise but the very things that corporations sought to produce? This story begins with the familiar indignities of starting a new job before spiralling outwards into a nightmare of institutional cruelty. Revisiting the themes of My Work is Not Yet Done , this story explores a world in which the mechanisms that make us suffer are indistinguishable from those that promise to alleviate our suffering, and even the desire for revenge can be put to work.
